title: When Automatic Captions Get Names Wrong
section: 讲话 / 报道 / 讲座
transcript:
Automatic captions have made recorded lectures easier to use, especially for students who study in a noisy room or who are still getting used to the lecturer's accent. The captions can look remarkably accurate across a full hour. But one university team wondered whether that overall impression concealed mistakes in the words that mattered most. A caption can get nearly every connecting word right and still make a technical explanation difficult to follow if it changes the name of a method.

To investigate, the team collected recordings from introductory lectures in several subjects. They prepared a reference transcript for each recording by checking it against the lecturer's slides and consulting the lecturer where the wording remained uncertain. Instead of giving every word equal weight, the researchers made a separate list of names and specialist terms and measured how often those items were rendered incorrectly. This allowed them to compare the figure a software provider might advertise with a figure that better represented a student's experience.

The largest gap appeared in courses that introduced unfamiliar terminology early. In one lecture, the system repeatedly replaced a researcher's surname with an ordinary English phrase. As a result, students who searched for the phrase could not find the recommended paper. Giving the captioning system a short course vocabulary list before processing the recording reduced this kind of mistake, even though the overall error rate changed very little.

The team cautioned that the recordings had been made with good microphones in fairly quiet rooms. A vocabulary list may help in a busy laboratory too, but the study did not establish how much it would help there. The researchers now want to repeat the comparison under less predictable recording conditions.

questions.prompt: What prompted the researchers to examine automatic captions?
options: An apparently high level of accuracy could hide important mistakes.
Students were unable to read captions on smaller screens.
Lecturers frequently used two languages in the same sentence.
Technical lectures usually lasted longer than the software allowed.
questions.answer: An apparently high level of accuracy could hide important mistakes.
questions.explanation: 团队怀疑整体看起来准确的字幕，可能在关键名字或专业术语上出错。

questions.prompt: How did the researchers evaluate captions in a way that reflected students' needs?
options: They tested how fast students could read the captions.
They counted errors on names and specialist terms separately.
They asked software providers to explain each mistake.
They compared only captions from lectures of the same length.
questions.answer: They counted errors on names and specialist terms separately.
questions.explanation: 团队把姓名和专业术语单独列出，专门统计这些词的错误率。

questions.prompt: What improved the captioning of unfamiliar words?
options: Removing rare words from the slides.
Giving the system a course vocabulary list.
Asking the lecturer to speak more slowly.
questions.answer: Giving the system a course vocabulary list.
questions.explanation: 录音处理前提供课程词汇表后，生僻术语或姓名被错误替换的情况减少。

questions.prompt: What remains uncertain after the study?
options: Whether captions can be corrected after publication.
Whether names are harder to caption than connecting words.
Whether students use subtitles when they study.
How well the method works with noisier recordings.
questions.answer: How well the method works with noisier recordings.
questions.explanation: 实验录音来自安静教室且麦克风质量好，尚未验证嘈杂环境下的改善幅度。
